title: Motion Graphs
summary: Builds a directed graph of captured clips and synthesized transitions; graph walks satisfy user constraints such as locomotion paths.
limitations: Transition thresholds require manual selection and can be laborious across diverse movements. Candidate comparison costs quadratically many frame pairs. Only nearby motions admit simple reliable blends; sparse connectivity and source-library coverage bound possible behaviors. Demonstrations do not establish unseen task composition or object-aware manipulation.
method: Constructs a directed graph whose edges are captured motion fragments and synthesized transitions. Candidate connections minimize aligned point-cloud distances over temporal windows, with floor-plane translation/yaw factored out. Locally similar windows are blended, constraint labels are propagated, and problematic graph portions are pruned. Branch-and-bound graph search then minimizes an application-specific additive objective; footplant constraints can be enforced after extraction.
conditions: A captured motion database, optional action/constraint labels, a desired planar path, and restrictions on action types along portions of the path.
data_split: No learned train/validation/test split: demonstrations reuse a finite motion library. Largest example has approximately 6,000 frames/200 seconds; other graphs contain about 3,000 frames.
metrics: Path-fitting objective measures deviation between requested and synthesized paths. Reports construction/search wall time and animation duration; no FID, semantic retrieval benchmark, or statistical user-study score.
evaluation: Section 5 demonstrates walking, sneaking, martial arts and constrained changes between these styles. A 12.8-second sneaking capture plus its mirror yields alternative paths. The walking Hello example needs 58.1 seconds computation for 54.9 seconds animation.
full_text_version: Primary author/proceedings PDF retrieved 2026-11-19; identity fixed by SHA256

title: DartControl: A Diffusion-Based Autoregressive Motion Model for Real-Time Text-Driven Motion Control
summary: Latent diffusion predicts motion primitives from history and current text; noise optimization or RL provides spatial control.
limitations: Short local history and a kinematic generative prior do not certify physical execution. HumanML3D subset differences matter for comparison. Goal-reaching results concern the demonstrated control setup, not general dexterous object manipulation or arbitrary scene-task completion.
method: Learns a history-conditioned motion-primitive VAE and text/history-conditioned latent diffusion model. Each primitive contains two history frames and eight generated frames, canonicalized around the pelvis. Scheduled autoregressive training mitigates rollout mismatch. Spatial control operates through latent-noise optimization, or a separately trained reinforcement-learning policy whose actions select latent noise; this differs from training a physics-based low-level humanoid controller.
conditions: An initial motion seed, an ordered stream of text prompts with durations, and optional goals, trajectories or scene geometry for the chosen control application.
data_split: BABEL training recordings train the default model; temporal composition evaluates its released validation set because its test set is unavailable. HumanML3D experiments use only records with available SMPL motion, excluding joint-only/mirrored sources; exact retained counts are not given in Appendix B.
metrics: FID, R-precision, MM-DIST and diversity assess segments; peak jerk and area under jerk assess 30-frame transition windows. Also reports latency, frames/second, memory, reach time/success, foot skating and foot-floor distance.
evaluation: Compares TEACH, DoubleTake, history-conditioned T2M-GPT and FlowMDM; profiles 5,000-frame generation and conducts perceptual comparisons. Optimization and RL goal-reaching are evaluated separately.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.3; Tables 1–4; Appendices B, E and G.

title: AMD: Autoregressive Motion Diffusion
summary: Introduces HumanLong3D and conditions iterative diffusion generation on current text plus previous text and action sequences.
limitations: Longer rollout depends on generated context and can accumulate error. A dataset-example split does not establish unseen skill-pair or actor generalization. Online estimated dance poses and newly collected motion have different provenance and should not be treated as uniform measured ground truth.
method: Autoregressively generates one diffusion-based motion segment per ordered text prompt. A context encoder combines the current prompt, the preceding prompt and preceding generated motion; a duration network predicts a categorical distribution over segment lengths. Training couples temporal motion context and denoising, rather than independently synthesizing clips and interpolating them afterward. The paper also builds HumanLong3D with coherence annotations and HumanMusic from online dance videos.
conditions: Ordered natural-language prompts and prior generated segment context; a music-conditioned variant uses audio features. Segment duration is predicted rather than assumed fixed at deployment.
data_split: HumanLong3D compound-motion experiment partitions examples into training/test/validation at 85/10/5 percent. Exact subject, source-recording or composition-ancestor separation is not specified. HumanML3D provides the short-motion benchmark; AIST++ and HumanMusic provide music experiments.
metrics: FID measures generated/reference feature-distribution distance; top-3 R-precision and multimodal distance measure text alignment; diversity and multimodality measure across-prompt and within-prompt variation. Music evaluation follows the cited dance protocol.
evaluation: Compares joint prediction, independent generation/interpolation and autoregressive prediction on HumanLong3D, alongside short text-to-motion baselines. The duration network covers approximately 2–9.8 seconds per segment in the implementation.
evidence_locator: Our Approach; Datasets and Evaluation Metrics; Comparisons on Compound Motion; Tables 1–3; Figure 1.

title: MultiAct: Long-Term 3D Human Motion Generation from Multiple Action Labels
summary: Recurrently conditions on prior motion and the next action label to generate transitions and long multi-action sequences.
limitations: Discrete action categories provide less detailed control than text or geometry. Recurrent generation is assessed on BABEL’s annotated transitions, and favorable feature scores do not certify foot contact, object consistency, or arbitrary physical task sequencing.
year_basis: First public preprint in December 2022; revised 2023.
publication_note: First public preprint in December 2022; revised 2023.
method: MultiAct recurrently predicts a transition and next action through MACVAE, a motion-and-action-conditioned variational autoencoder. Separate latent variables encode the previous-motion context and current action. A face-front canonicalization removes heading and location while retaining the gravity relationship, avoiding the floor-orientation loss caused by full root zeroing. An ACTOR model produces the initial action before recurrent continuation.
conditions: A sequence of discrete action labels and previous generated motion; transition and action durations are part of the sampled training/generation setting, not free-form language understanding.
data_split: Uses BABEL training split for learning and released validation split for testing, extracting alternating action and transition intervals. Test previous-motion inputs are unseen examples; no independently held-out action-pair split or new proportional split is declared in the main paper.
metrics: FID against training and test feature distributions, top-1/top-5 action recognition, diversity across actions and multimodality within actions. Transition FID and action accuracy are also measured along long rollouts.
evaluation: Compares MACVAE to action-conditioned generation combined with interpolation or a motion-transition model. Ablations remove separate latents and vary canonicalization or previous-motion input; long-horizon plots track action accuracy and transition distribution.
evidence_locator: MACVAE and Long-Term Motion Generation sections; Datasets; Evaluation metrics; Tables 1–3; Figures 4–6.

title: SALAD: Skeleton-aware Latent Diffusion for Text-driven Motion Generation and Editing
summary: Models joint-frame-word relationships and edits generated motion by cross-attention modulation without explicit user masks.
limitations: Diversity remains limited and competes with fidelity. Only a single person and bounded text/motion lengths are modeled. The authors explicitly state that editing real recorded motions is not directly addressed; attention preservation ratings are not an exact frame/joint invariance guarantee.
method: Trains a skeleto-temporal VAE with skeletal pooling and temporal compression, preserving joint/frame structure in latent space. A denoiser separately models skeletal, temporal and word-level relations. At inference, cross-attention maps support word swapping, attention reweighting and left/right attention mirroring without training a dedicated editor or requiring an explicit edit mask.
conditions: Natural-language descriptions and requested sequence length; editing manipulates the attention of a source generation using changed words or weights, rather than directly accepting arbitrary captured motion.
data_split: HumanML3D and KIT-ML motion sequences are mirrored and divided into training/test/validation at 80/15/5 percent. No unseen action-combination or subject-disjoint protocol is reported. The editing study uses 15 videos per method and 16 participants.
metrics: FID measures motion feature distributions; R-precision and MM-Dist measure text alignment; diversity and multimodality measure variation. Reconstruction evaluation reports motion-feature errors and parameter counts. Editing ratings measure preservation, target-text alignment and overall quality on five-point scales.
evaluation: Table 1 averages 20 evaluations with 95 percent confidence intervals. Compares generation with diffusion/token baselines and editing with MDM and MotionFix; ablates guidance, parameterization, VAE and FiLM components.
evidence_locator: Sections 3, 4.1–4.5 and 5; Tables 1–4; Figures 3 and 7; Supplement A–C.

title: AMD:Anatomical Motion Diffusion with Interpretable Motion Decomposition and Fusion
summary: Parses complex text into anatomical scripts and fuses script and text guidance in diffusion.
limitations: Reference quality and database breadth directly limit generation; LLM decomposition can add excessive constraints and reduce multimodality. Complex language subsets are not equivalent to systematically withheld skill combinations, and demonstrated ball/grab semantics do not imply generated physical object trajectories.
method: Uses fine-tuned ChatGPT-3.5 to decompose complex descriptions into concise anatomical scripts. Sentence-BERT retrieves reference motions for these scripts. Two diffusion branches model the original prompt and the prompt plus scripts/reference actions; a Bernoulli fusion schedule switches their contributions during denoising. This is the anatomical AMD, distinct from Autoregressive Motion Diffusion despite the shared acronym.
conditions: Original text plus automatically decomposed scripts and retrieved reference-motion tokens. Retrieval depends on a motion-text database; masked-joint and in-between demonstrations additionally constrain unedited motion.
data_split: Evaluates HumanML3D and KIT-ML and constructs SLCD1/SLCD2 complex-language test subsets from HumanML3D. The reviewed experiment text does not specify subset cardinalities, a new train/validation/test proportion, or a composition-ancestor exclusion protocol.
metrics: Top-3 R-precision, FID, multimodal distance, diversity and multimodality. Complex-text tables use ground-truth motion lengths; evaluation repeats 20 times, except multimodality five times, with 95 percent confidence intervals.
evaluation: Compares against MDM, TM2T, MotionDiffuse, T2M-GPT and other text-motion systems. Ablations remove decomposition or reference information and vary fusion probability. Editing demonstrations fix endpoint quarters or lower-body joints.
evidence_locator: Text Decomposition; Motion Diffusion and Fusion; Training and Inference; Experiments; Tables 1–3 and Figures 5–7; Conclusion limitation paragraph.

title: Infinite Motion: Extended Motion Generation via Long Text Instructions
summary: Extends and reassembles text-motion data, using timestamped text for long narrative generation, local editing and independent sequence splicing.
limitations: Interpolation and foot refinement can alter source motion. Cross-source stitching requires consistent body representation. Reported benchmark improvement does not establish semantic dependency correctness, collision freedom, or independent withheld-composition generalization; split ancestry needs an additional audit.
method: Builds HumanML3D-Extend by selecting compatible short motions, aligning root positions, interpolating boundary frames and refining feet using quadratic Bezier curves. Text descriptions receive cumulative timestamps. The generation pipeline fine-tunes MLD on extended sequences, then trains a timestamp stitcher that denoises transitions between independently supplied motion segments. Applications include timed local editing, interactive text modification and sequence splicing.
conditions: Long text with temporal information and, for stitching/editing, existing motion segments or unchanged context. Timestamps are explicit control signals rather than automatically inferred task boundaries.
data_split: Experiments name HumanML3D-Extend train/test sets and also evaluate its trained model on original HumanML3D test sequences. The reviewed full text does not state numeric split proportions or demonstrate source-recording/ancestor isolation before reassembly.
metrics: FID, top-1/2/3 R-precision, MM-Dist, diversity and multimodality assess generation. APE and AVE assess root/body positional and variance differences; transition distance measures consecutive-pose jumps in body-local coordinates.
evaluation: Tables compare short- and extended-benchmark results, several stitch lengths and DoubleTake. Extended examples commonly last 30–40 seconds and contain four or five actions; these are reassembled sequences, not newly captured continuous performance.
evidence_locator: Section 3 dataset construction and generation; Algorithm 1; Sections 4.1–4.4 and 5; Tables 2–5; conclusion limitations.

title: MMM: Generative Masked Motion Model
summary: Text-conditioned masked motion tokens support in-betweening, body-part changes and long sequence synthesis.
limitations: Fine details for exceptionally long single descriptions remain difficult because training motions reach at most about 196 frames. The model does not support multi-person interactions. Token-space preservation and attractive stitching examples do not establish object-state continuity or systematically unseen skill composition.
method: Learns a VQ motion tokenizer with an 8,192-entry factorized codebook, then trains a text-conditioned transformer to reconstruct randomly masked tokens. Iterative parallel decoding retains confident tokens and remasks uncertain ones. Arbitrary temporal masks enable in-betweening; long generation first synthesizes prompt-specific segments and fills transition tokens. Upper-body editing uses separately pretrained upper/lower tokenizers and specialized conditioning rather than arbitrary joint editing in the default whole-body tokenizer.
conditions: Text prompts, requested motion length, and optional visible motion tokens or an upper/lower-body editing partition.
data_split: HumanML3D and KIT-ML use motion-sequence training/validation/test proportions of 80/5/15 percent, following the T2M protocol. No subject-disjoint or held-out semantic-combination split is reported for the composition demonstrations.
metrics: FID, top-k R-precision, text-motion multimodal distance, diversity and multimodality use pretrained T2M embeddings. Average inference time per sentence (AITS) and length-dependent timing assess efficiency.
evaluation: Quantitative generation evaluation repeats 20 times with 95 percent confidence intervals. Tables 1–2 compare benchmark generation; timing uses the same RTX A5000. Qualitative comparisons show in-betweening, upper-body replacement and sequential stories, with masking/iteration ablations.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.2, 4, 5 and 6; Tables 1–2; Supplement B and J.

title: MoMask: Generative Masked Modeling of 3D Human Motions
summary: Hierarchical residual quantization and masked token generation provide a discrete motion prior with text-guided temporal inpainting.
limitations: The authors report limited diversity, a required target length, and difficulty with rapidly changing root motion such as spinning. Tokenization and temporal inpainting do not establish cross-dataset skill transfer, object interaction or physical task completion.
method: Tokenizes motion with hierarchical residual vector quantization: a base code sequence captures coarse content and subsequent code layers encode residual detail. A text-conditioned masked transformer iteratively predicts the base layer; a residual transformer generates the remaining quantization layers. Classifier-free guidance is applied to both. Temporal inpainting keeps selected reference intervals and regenerates the remainder under text conditioning.
conditions: A sentence and sequence length, or a text instruction plus reference temporal regions for inpainting. The base representation is frame-sequence oriented rather than an explicit independent joint-token interface.
data_split: HumanML3D and KIT-ML are mirrored and partitioned into training/test/validation at 80/15/5 percent. These ordinary motion-language splits are not described as withheld composition-pair or subject splits.
metrics: FID assesses real/generated motion feature distributions; top-k R-precision and multimodal distance assess semantic alignment; multimodality assesses variation for one prompt. VQ reconstruction errors, inference cost and user preference provide supplementary evaluation.
evaluation: Table 1 compares text generation against diffusion and token models. Inference-time comparisons use the same Nvidia 2080Ti; ablations vary quantization layers, dropout and decoding. Figure 6 shows temporally specified text-guided inpainting.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4 and 5; Table 1; Figures 5–6; quantization ablations and Discussion limitations.

title: Executing Your Commands via Motion Diffusion in Latent Space
summary: MLD compresses motions with a VAE before conditional latent diffusion, substantially reducing denoising cost.
limitations: Sequence latents do not expose a direct joint/frame editing correspondence. The stated maximum sequence length remains bounded by the dataset; articulated body generation does not cover detailed hands or faces. Efficient benchmark generation alone does not validate temporal skill composition or object-conditioned behavior.
method: First trains a transformer-based motion VAE to reconstruct sequences in a compact latent space, then freezes that representation and trains conditional denoising diffusion over its latents. Frozen CLIP text embeddings or learned action embeddings condition the denoiser; classifier-free guidance balances fidelity and variation. The decoder maps generated latents back to whole motion sequences, reducing denoising cost relative to raw-frame diffusion.
conditions: Text plus sequence length, a predefined action category, or an empty condition for unconditional generation. Future motion is output rather than a required trajectory condition.
data_split: Text experiments inherit HumanML3D and KIT protocols. UESTC action evaluation reports FIDtrain and FIDtest, whereas HumanAct12 reports training-reference FID. The main text does not restate all numeric split proportions or add a semantic-combination holdout.
metrics: FID, R-precision, MM-Dist, diversity and multimodality measure generation. MPJPE, Procrustes-aligned MPJPE and acceleration error assess VAE reconstruction; AITS and elapsed time assess computational efficiency; action accuracy assesses action-conditioned samples.
evaluation: Text evaluation repeats 20 times with 95 percent confidence intervals. Tables compare text, action and unconditional tasks; VAE and latent-dimension ablations distinguish reconstruction from diffusion quality.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.5, 5 and 6; Tables 1–5.
full_text_version: Primary author/proceedings PDF retrieved 2026-11-19; identity fixed by SHA256

title: MotionDiffuse: Text-Driven Human Motion Generation with Diffusion Model
summary: Text-conditioned diffusion models human motion and provides a foundation for fine-grained guided synthesis.
limitations: Part/time noise composition is demonstrated under chosen masks and intervals, not an arbitrary task dependency benchmark. Denoising cost is substantial and the kinematic objective does not enforce object dynamics or guaranteed collision/contact consistency. A familiar caption split does not isolate unseen skill pairs.
method: Applies a denoising diffusion model directly to human motion, with a text encoder and efficient linear-transformer motion decoder. Timestep/text-dependent stylization blocks modulate denoising. For body-part control, predicted noises from separate text prompts are masked and combined with a consistency correction; time-varying control similarly composes padded interval-specific noises. These operations reuse a trained prior without separately captured composite supervision.
conditions: Natural-language description and motion length; optional descriptions assigned to body masks or time intervals. Action-conditioned experiments replace action indices with their semantic descriptions.
data_split: Uses HumanML3D and KIT-ML benchmark test sets, plus HumanAct12 and UESTC action experiments. The reviewed full-text experimental description inherits dataset protocols without restating numerical sequence-split proportions or a systematic withheld-combination split.
metrics: FID and R-precision are principal metrics; MM-Dist evaluates text-motion feature distance, diversity and multimodality evaluate sample variation. Retrieval compares a matching caption to 31 randomly selected distractors; reports top-1/2/3 accuracy.
evaluation: Tables 1–2 evaluate text generation with real motion lengths and 20 repetitions/95 percent confidence intervals. Additional action and manipulation experiments and architecture ablations test pretrained CLIP and efficient attention.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.2–3.5 and 4.1–4.3; Equations 10–11; Tables 1–3.

title: Skeleton-Aware Networks for Deep Motion Retargeting
summary: Skeleton-aware convolutions and pooling map homeomorphic skeletons into a common primal-skeleton motion latent space.
limitations: Compatible topology and end-effectors restrict scope. Retargeting preserves existing motion semantics and is not independent skill synthesis. Positional accuracy does not guarantee exact contact, stable physics, finger dexterity or validity for a new robot with different actuation.
method: Introduces skeleton-aware convolution, pooling and unpooling operators that respect articulated adjacency. Homeomorphic skeleton graphs reduce to a shared primal structure, permitting separate encoders/decoders to exchange latent motion across skeletons with different bone counts and proportions. Unpaired retargeting combines reconstruction, cycle/latent consistency, adversarial realism and end-effector constraints; forward kinematics connects rotations with positional supervision.
conditions: A source skeletal motion, source offsets and target skeleton offsets/structure. The method assumes compatible main limbs/end effectors and a graph homeomorphism, not arbitrary unrelated anatomy.
data_split: Mixamo group A contains 24 characters: 20 train and four unseen test characters; evaluation uses 106 test motions. Cross-structural group B has five characters, four train and one test. Motions are available across characters for quantitative ground truth although training is unpaired.
metrics: Retargeting error averages Euclidean joint-position discrepancy to target ground truth, normalized by skeleton height; Table 2 scales this by 1,000. Reconstruction and denoising experiments also compare conventional versus skeleton-aware operators.
evaluation: Compares NKN, PMnet, rotation copying and a CycleGAN adaptation; ablates shared latents, operators and adversarial loss. Cross-structural experiments insert joints along existing branches rather than creating new functional limbs.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–5, 6.1–6.3; Equation 10; Tables 1–2; Figures 7–10.

title: Learning a bidirectional mapping between human whole-body motion and natural language using deep recurrent neural networks
summary: Sequence-to-sequence RNN learns shared continuous language/motion representations without manual motion segmentation.
limitations: Round-trip evaluation inherits errors and biases of the learned captioner, so it is not independent physical or motion-fidelity evidence. The authors discuss ambiguity and why positional MSE is insufficient. Random recording splits do not establish unseen skill-combination, subject or object-task generalization.
method: Trains two probabilistic sequence-to-sequence recurrent models, one mapping whole-body motion to words and the other mapping language to motion. Motion uses the common Master Motor Map representation with root and joint parameters, while the motion decoder predicts a mixture distribution and stopping probability. Multiple hypotheses can be sampled and ranked by model likelihood, without explicit action segmentation.
conditions: A motion sequence for captioning or a natural-language sentence for motion synthesis. This is a bidirectional translation framework, not a multimodal task planner.
data_split: Uses KIT Motion-Language release 2016-10-10. After filtering, 2,846 motions and 6,187 captions remain. Random training/validation/test split is 80/10/10 percent; every motion and all associated captions stay together. Training uses offset downsampling augmentation.
metrics: Corpus BLEU, with up to four-gram matches, evaluates generated descriptions. Text-to-motion is evaluated by recaptioning generated motion and computing BLEU, including relative retention against the motion-captioning baseline; likelihood ranks hypotheses.
evaluation: Tables 2–4 report caption and round-trip scores on training/test sets. Qualitative examples include locomotion, wiping, kicking and handed waving. Latent-space experiments explore how semantic changes affect representations.
evidence_locator: Sections 3, 4.1–4.3, 5.1, 5.3.3 and 5.4.3; Tables 2–4; Figure 8.

title: InterAct: Advancing Large-Scale Versatile 3D Human-Object Interaction Generation
summary: Consolidates HOI sources, refines artifacts and hands, augments under contact invariance, and benchmarks six generation/completion tasks.
limitations: Synthetic augmentation is not new motion capture. Hands are corrected under assumptions suitable for grasp conformity rather than high dexterity. Contact/penetration improvements and text-feature scores do not establish force consistency, independent ancestor-disjoint composition or arbitrary object generalization.
method: Consolidates seven whole-body HOI sources with common surface markers, object BPS geometry and checked human/GPT-4 text annotations. Optimization corrects body/contact artifacts, then hands; augmentation shifts object trajectories and realigns humans while preserving near-contact distances. A transformer diffusion baseline jointly predicts motion and marker-to-object contact vectors, with interaction-aware text features and optional contact guidance. Six tasks distinguish language generation, inpainting, prediction and simulated imitation.
conditions: Task-dependent text/action labels, object shape and trajectories, human motion, past HOI or complete reference interactions. Object-conditioned human generation uses future object motion as an input and is not unconstrained object-trajectory generation.
data_split: Supplement C: text/action generation partitions each source 9:1 train/test; object-to-human separates 168 training and 29 unseen test objects; human-to-object uses 10:1. Prediction trains on 90 percent and tests on the held-out BEHAVE 10 percent.
metrics: FID, R-precision, MM-Dist, diversity/multimodality; penetration depth/contact ratio; marker error, foot sliding, contact precision/recall/accuracy/F1; object translation/quaternion error; imitation success.
evaluation: Tables 2–8 separate correction, generation and conditional prediction. Corrected versus raw PhysHOI imitation is demonstrated on four selected sequences over 2,048 environments; this is a narrower experiment than full-corpus executability.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4 and 5.1–5.5; Tables 2–8; Supplement C.2–C.7 and E.

title: InterDiff: Generating 3D Human-Object Interactions with Physics-Informed Diffusion
summary: Interaction diffusion forecasts human/object motion and a physics-informed correction predictor refines denoised interactions.
limitations: Intuitive physics is a learned correction, not a dynamics solver. Skeleton-only contacts are ill-defined and omit penetration/contact losses. Best-of-many oracle scores should not be read as single-output accuracy; short forecasting and GRAB visualization do not prove text-conditioned task composition.
method: Predicts future human-object interaction using a transformer diffusion model conditioned on past interaction and object geometry. A correction scheduler identifies likely penetration or loss of contact and chooses a reference frame attached to a human surface marker or the ground. A separate spatial-temporal graph predictor models simpler object dynamics in those coordinates; its prediction is transformed back and blended into denoising. Components train separately.
conditions: Past human/object motion plus object shape. Typical BEHAVE setup gives ten historical frames and predicts 25 future frames, with autoregressive continuation for longer horizons; no text condition is required.
data_split: Uses official BEHAVE train/test partition. On skeleton-based HOI, 18,352 twenty-frame sequences include 582 evaluation sequences with unseen objects; predicts ten future from ten past frames. Cross-dataset experiment trains on BEHAVE and evaluates GRAB without fine-tuning.
metrics: MPJPE-H and MPJPE-O measure global human joints/object keypoints in millimeters; translation error is L2, rotation error uses quaternion difference, and penetration measures object vertices inside the human. Best-of-many evaluation explicitly selects lowest candidate errors.
evaluation: Tables compare InterRNN, InterVAE and skeletal prediction baselines. A 100-frame rollout tests long-term prediction; user comparisons assess physical fidelity, while correction/reference ablations probe the inductive bias.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.2 and 4.1–4.4; Tables 1–4; Figures 3 and 7.

title: GOAL: Generating 4D Whole-Body Motion for Hand-Object Grasping
summary: GNet predicts a whole-body goal grasp and MNet produces approach motion with coordinated hands, head and body.
limitations: Approach distance is bounded and longer navigation remains future work. The method lacks full surrounding-scene awareness and focuses on grasp acquisition, not subsequent object manipulation or release. Overlapping window counts must not be mistaken for independent captured sequences.
method: Generates a whole-body grasping goal with GNet, a conditional generative model conditioned on object geometry/pose, then uses autoregressive MNet to produce approach motion from the starting body state. Interaction-aware vertex offsets connect body and object geometry; optimization refines both goal grasp and generated motion using predicted Euclidean-space interaction features. MNet generates ten future frames per iteration and rolls forward to the grasp.
conditions: An object mesh, its position/orientation, and a starting human pose/shape roughly 0.5–1.5 meters away. No free-text command or future object trajectory is required.
data_split: Trains on GRAB right-hand stable grasps and approach subsequences. Supplement reports approximately 160K/26K/12.5K static frames and 40K/7K/3K motion windows for train/test/validation. Windows contain ten past, one current and ten future frames; exact source-group holdout membership is not restated.
metrics: Static goals and generated motions receive five-point perceptual ratings for body realism, foot-ground contact, grasp and head orientation. MNet horizon ablations report body/hand/foot vertex distances and pose/translation reconstruction errors. Foot sliding counts frames whose selected ground-near vertex moves over one centimeter.
evaluation: Compares GNet before/after optimization and ground-truth grasps, and studies MNet output horizon. Generated motion has 13.7 percent sliding frames versus 6.7 percent for ground truth under its stated metric.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.5, 4.1–4.3 and 5; Tables 1–3; Supplement 6 Data Preparation.

title: CIRCLE: Capture In Rich Contextual Environments
summary: Captures real human movement in perceived virtual scenes and learns scene-conditioned full-body reaching.
limitations: The authors note persistent collisions and foot sliding. A nearly static baseline can misleadingly score well on sliding. VR capture does not provide physical contact reactions, and task-held-out reaching does not imply unseen scenes, dexterous grasping or object dynamics.
method: Captures full-body reaching while participants view virtual environments through a VR headset. Real capture space remains empty, while the simulator supplies exact scene geometry and rendered observations. A scene-aware transformer refines an initialized motion between a start pose and target wrist location, using local body/scene features from BPS or pretrained PointNet++ encodings. Training combines root, joint position, rotation and forward-kinematics losses.
conditions: Initial body pose, scene geometry and a target right-hand/wrist position; this is contextual reaching, not dynamic object manipulation. Virtual scene contact has no corresponding physical object force feedback.
data_split: 3,018 reaching sequences: random split has 2,565 train/453 test; task split has 2,578 train/440 test, holding out start/goal region pairs (109 training and 19 test tasks). Five subjects perform about ten hours across nine scenes.
metrics: Success means final wrist within ten centimeters of target. Also measures distance to goal, cumulative scene collision depth, foot sliding, mean vertex/joint-position errors, root translation and joint-orientation discrepancy.
evaluation: Tables 2–3 compare scene-conditioned variants, a no-scene baseline and GOAL modified to receive a ground-truth goal pose. All use the same data; task-held-out results degrade, and scene features improve reaching/collision behavior.
evidence_locator: Sections 3, 4, 5.1–5.3 and 6; Tables 2–3; Figure 6.

title: Compositional Human-Scene Interaction Synthesis with Semantic Control
summary: COINS encodes body surface points and objects in a joint latent space, permitting multiple atomic action-object pairs without corresponding composite training examples.
limitations: Objects not explicitly conditioned can be ignored, requiring scene-SDF postprocessing. Hand contact is limited by noisy estimated hands in training data. Static semantic/geometry consistency does not establish transitions, force balance, object manipulation or long-horizon task execution.
method: COINS synthesizes static human-scene interactions with action-object-instance semantics. PelvisVAE samples global pelvis placement; BodyVAE generates local body vertices and contact, followed by optimization. For composite interactions, separate atomic pelvis distributions are reconciled through latent optimization; action-specific contact statistics produce body-part attention masks, combining independently learned atomic constraints without training on composite examples.
conditions: A 3D scene and one or more explicit action/object-instance pairs, such as sitting on a chair while touching a table. Generated output is a body configuration, not a continuous interaction sequence.
data_split: PROX-S annotates about 32K frames from 43 PROX recordings in 12 indoor scenes. Four named scenes are held out (MPH16, MPH1Library, N0SittingBooth, N3OpenArea), with eight scenes for training; evaluates about 150 action/object-instance combinations.
metrics: Semantic contact compares action-weighted contact to a threshold from training data. Non-collision is the fraction of vertices with nonnegative scene SDF. Diversity uses 50-cluster entropy and distance to centers; user studies assess naturalness and semantic agreement.
evaluation: Compares adapted PiGraph-X and POSA-style interaction baselines and atomic/composite variants. The composite experiment explicitly tests composing interactions learned individually, making its composition evidence narrower but more direct than ordinary text generation.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.2–3.3, 4.1–4.4; Supplement B.1 and D; semantic contact definition and composite-generation equations.

title: CORE4D: A 4D Human-Object-Human Interaction Dataset for Collaborative Object REarrangement
summary: Combines real collaborative object rearrangement recordings with collaboration retargeting to additional object shapes.
limitations: Captures are indoors and synthetic examples lack visual streams. Main text says 37 real objects, while the supplement lists 38. Retargeted descendants are not independent captures; object-path synthesis and simulated box lifting do not establish general text-driven collaborative control. Supplementary F.2 calls Cacc accuracy but describes a contact-error percentage, whereas the main table marks higher as better; that source ambiguity is retained rather than silently resolved.
method: Combines captured two-person object rearrangement with synthetic retargeting to new object shapes. Real acquisition combines inertial/optical body tracking, gloves, object tracking and multiple camera views. Synthetic generation iterates contact-candidate selection and contact-guided human-object retargeting, scoring plausibility with a learned discriminator plus interpenetration penalties. The dataset has roughly 1K captured and 10K synthetic collaborative sequences.
conditions: Two human bodies, an object and its geometry; forecasting uses past collaborative interaction, while synthesis benchmarks condition on object motion. These inputs differ from text-only generation.
data_split: Supplement Table 3 lists 482 real and 10,016 synthetic training sequences, 225 real S1 sequences for seen objects, and 255 real S2 sequences for novel objects. Synthetic examples never enter testing. Humanoid application separately uses 16 training boxes/504 clips, with six boxes/386 clips held out.
metrics: Forecasting measures MPJPE, object translation/rotation errors, five-centimeter-threshold hand contact and penetration. Synthesis uses root-relative joint/vertex errors and FID. Supplement F defines vertex error on humans, unlike the main-text object-vertex wording; this inconsistency remains unresolved.
evaluation: Compares MDM/InterDiff/CAHMP forecasting and MDM/CHOIS/OMOMO synthesis; synthetic-data and humanoid lifting experiments test augmentation utility.
evidence_locator: Main Sections 3.1–3.4, 4.1–4.4 and 5, Tables 2–6; official Supplement E/Table 3, F.1–F.2, I.1–I.2. Supplemental URL: https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2025/supplemental/Liu_CORE4D_A_4D_CVPR_2025_supplemental.pdf
full_text_version: Primary author/proceedings PDF retrieved 2026-11-19; identity fixed by SHA256

title: Inter-X: Towards Versatile Human-Human Interaction Analysis
summary: Captured full-body interactions with hand gestures and detailed part-level text support perceptual and generative benchmarking.
limitations: Indoor non-professional captures omit facial expressions, and atomic interactions dominate rather than long uninterrupted interaction chains. Most task splits are sequence-level, so they should not be described as actor-disjoint. Rich annotations and baseline generation do not establish unseen compositional pairs or physically certified interpersonal contacts.
method: Captures two-person whole-body motion including hands using optical motion capture and fits SMPL-X sequences. Adds detailed text, action classes, actor/reactor order, relationships and personality annotations. Rather than proposing one new universal generator, it adapts existing text/action generation, reaction, recognition and captioning models into a common interaction benchmark, preserving both participants’ global translations to maintain relative geometry.
conditions: Downstream task determines input: text, action category, actor motion, interaction motion, or relationship/personality attributes. Human-human interaction and expressive hand motion are central; dynamic object manipulation is not the primary task.
data_split: Main generation experiments partition sequences into train/test/validation at 80/15/5 percent. Personality prediction explicitly uses person-ID splits with the same proportions, a separate protocol that must not be attributed to all tasks.
metrics: Generation uses FID, diversity, multimodality, top-1/2/3 R-precision and MM-Dist. Action tasks include recognition accuracy; captioning adds BLEU, ROUGE, CIDEr and BERTScore; personality regression uses R-squared.
evaluation: Compares adapted diffusion/VAE interaction models, action generators, reaction generators and skeleton classifiers. Experiments and ablations emphasize expressive hand representation and actor/reactor asymmetry; qualitative comparisons contrast Inter-X and InterHuman-trained outputs.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–5, 6.1–6.4 and 7; Tables 1–5; Supplement A.1–A.4.

title: FineMotion: A Dataset and Benchmark with both Spatial and Temporal Annotation for Fine-grained Motion Generation and Editing
summary: Adds aligned body-part descriptions for motion snippets and complete sequences, supporting fine-grained generation and spatial/temporal editing.
limitations: Automatically inferred language can retain pose-estimation/model biases despite stronger grounding than caption-only expansion. Temporal editing is easier than spatial editing under this representation, explicitly left for future work. Dataset enrichment does not establish independent new actions or physically valid object interactions.
method: Produces fine-grained motion language through temporal segmentation, PoseFix-based pose-pair change descriptions, human correction of a small subset, and Gemini conversion of ordered snippet descriptions into coherent body-part-motion paragraphs. FineMotion contains 21,346 human and 420,968 automatic snippet descriptions plus whole-motion paragraphs. Baseline MDM, T2M-GPT and MoMask are adapted to coarse and detailed text using T5-Base to avoid CLIP truncation.
conditions: Coarse text optionally accompanied by temporally aligned detailed snippet descriptions or paragraphs. Temporal editing replaces descriptions and regenerates corresponding motion; the dataset supplies language rather than new independent motion capture.
data_split: Inherits HumanML3D sequence partitions: 80 percent training, five percent validation and 15 percent test. Human-annotated snippets cover roughly five percent of motions. The paper does not declare a separately held-out body-part-combination or actor protocol.
metrics: FID assesses motion distributions; top-1/2/3 R-precision and MM-Dist assess semantic alignment; diversity and multimodality assess variation. Annotation validity and human-versus-automatic detailed-text settings are compared separately.
evaluation: Tables test coarse-only and coarse-plus-detail training/testing, different automatic/human descriptions and model families. Editing examples demonstrate zero-shot temporal changes, while supplementary experiments analyze annotation granularity and component choices.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1.1–3.1.3, 3.2, 4.1–4.5; Table 2; Supplement 16 limitations.

title: Learning Generalizable Human Motion Generator with Reinforcement Learning
summary: Uses reinforcement learning and contrastive text-motion rewards on paired data and synthetic text-only prompts to improve generalization.
limitations: Reward models themselves are trained on limited paired data and prioritize coarse semantic alignment over fine motion. Optimizing learned alignment can exploit evaluator biases. Synthetic prompt generalization does not by itself establish unseen physical skills, object-state consistency, or independent contact-quality improvement.
method: Fine-tunes a supervised T2M-GPT motion-token generator with PPO, treating autoregressive token production as a Markov decision process. Rewards use pretrained contrastive text/motion encoders: generated-motion distance to text, and optionally to paired ground-truth motion. An LLM decomposes existing captions into meta motions, recombines them into novel descriptions and uses human filtering to remove implausible combinations. Synthetic prompts need no paired motion for RL fine-tuning.
conditions: A textual motion description; optional paired motion contributes an additional reward during training. This is reward-based generator adaptation, not human preference annotation or physical environment execution.
data_split: Benchmarks evaluate HumanML3D and KIT-ML test sets following their standard evaluation protocol. Synthetic descriptions have separate training/test prompt subsets, but the reviewed text does not state numerical partition proportions or a constituent-skill exclusion rule.
metrics: Top-1/2/3 R-precision, FID, MM-Dist and diversity use pretrained feature spaces. Human evaluations rank motions on paired-test, unpaired-training and unpaired-test prompts; quantitative tables repeat 20 evaluations for confidence intervals.
evaluation: Compares T2M-GPT baseline and MoMask, studies synthetic-data scaling and reward components, and shows qualitative novel-description examples. These tests probe transfer to recombined language beyond paired supervision.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1, 4.1–4.3, 5 and 6; Tables 1–3; Figures 3 and 5.

title: BEHAVE: Dataset and Method for Tracking Human Object Interactions
summary: Multi-view RGB-D body-object interaction data with body/object fits and contacts across everyday objects and locations.
limitations: Known object geometry, RGB-D acquisition and fitted supervision constrain applicability. Occlusion and noisy point clouds remain relevant; contact annotations are not measured force or friction labels. The dataset supports HOI studies but does not itself demonstrate generative composition, task execution or continuous collision-free motion.
method: Introduces RGB-D recordings and fitted body/object/contact annotations for natural full-body object interaction. The method jointly registers SMPL and a prescanned rigid object to multi-view depth observations. Neural predictions provide human-surface correspondence, object orientation and explicit contact correspondences, which enter optimization to align body/object meshes rather than fitting them independently. The released fits are pseudo-ground truth from this capture/optimization pipeline.
conditions: Multi-view RGB-D, human/object segmentation and known rigid object mesh; tracking estimates human pose/shape, object pose and contact. This is observation-conditioned reconstruction, not text-driven motion generation.
data_split: Experiments compare reconstruction on the dataset and its reference annotations. The reviewed main paper does not state explicit train/test sequence counts, proportions or actor/object-disjoint partition membership; later papers’ official splits should not be retroactively inferred here.
metrics: Human SMPL vertex-to-vertex error and object vertex-to-vertex error are reported in centimeters. Qualitative contact plausibility supplements geometric error; tables ablate orientation and contact terms and compare body registration.
evaluation: Compares PHOSA adapted to its input setup, IPNet and LoopReg, then tests learned object orientation and contact fitting. The authors note that contact removal can produce conspicuous floating despite small differences in aggregate vertex error.
evidence_locator: Sections 3, 4.1–4.4 and 5.1–5.4; Tables 1–3; Figures 3–5.

title: BABEL: Bodies, Action and Behavior with English Labels
summary: Adds sequence and temporally localized action language to AMASS, supporting action understanding and temporal composition.
limitations: Labels derive from annotator interpretation of body-only captures; some object/social semantics lack tracked corresponding entities. Long-tail categories and ambiguous boundaries complicate learning. Overlapping actions and source recordings require ancestry-aware evaluation before claiming unseen combinations or independent cross-dataset composition.
method: Adds sequence-level and temporally localized English action labels to AMASS motion. Annotators identify all simultaneous actions and label transitions; raw descriptions are embedded with Word2Vec, clustered and manually organized into 260 action categories, allowing multiple category memberships. The paper analyzes co-occurrence and temporal transitions and benchmarks skeleton-based action recognition using an adapted 2s-AGCN joint stream.
conditions: Body motion is the input to recognition; language/action intervals are annotations. Transition graphs describe observed category statistics rather than an evaluated continuous generative policy.
data_split: Original recognition study randomly partitions 13,220 source sequences into 60 percent train, 20 percent validation and 20 percent test. Evaluates 60- and 120-category subsets; action segments are further chunked into five-second sequences. Split is sequence-level, not claimed actor-disjoint.
metrics: Top-1 and Top-5 recognition accuracy; Top-1-norm averages per-category accuracy to expose long-tail bias. Descriptive analysis counts simultaneous-action pairs and temporally adjacent transitions; these counts are not generation-quality scores.
evaluation: Compares standard cross-entropy and class-balanced focal-loss training. Reports substantial performance degradation when expanding categories, highlighting the challenge of rare actions. Examples and random walks illustrate plausible action ordering, not verified generated body trajectories.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.4, 4.1–4.2 and 5; Tables 2–3; BABEL action recognition splits and Metrics paragraphs.

title: The KIT Motion-Language Dataset
summary: Aggregates mocap in a capture-independent representation with crowdsourced natural-language descriptions.
limitations: Coverage reflects original capture distributions and volunteer annotations, with differing detail, grammar and interpretation. Body-only motion does not supply tracked manipulated objects or scenes. A standardized motion representation enables reuse but does not guarantee compositional supervision, independent skill holdouts or physics labels.
method: Aggregates optical motion capture from KIT and CMU and converts it into the capture-independent Master Motor Map representation. A WebGL interface lets volunteers inspect animated motion and write English descriptions. Annotation selection starts with unannotated recordings, then uses language-model perplexity to prioritize unusual or inconsistent descriptions. Releases preserve original motion, converted motion, captions and provenance metadata with dated dataset versions.
conditions: No single generative model is proposed. The resource pairs full-body motion recordings with sentence descriptions and links them to source-database identities for downstream motion-language research.
data_split: The authors explicitly choose not to define a canonical train/validation/test split because researchers may use different subsets. October 2016 release contains 3,911 recordings from 111 subjects and 6,278 captions; downstream papers’ splits are separate choices.
metrics: Dataset statistics include duration, vocabulary, annotation counts and participant distribution. Four-gram language-model perplexity measures annotation surprise for collection/quality control; it is not a motion-generation accuracy or semantic-composition metric.
evaluation: Evaluates and documents the annotation workflow, motion-format conversion and dataset coverage rather than comparing synthesized motions under a fixed benchmark. Source metadata permits additional subject/capture information to be retrieved where available.
evidence_locator: Sections III–IV; Section V.A Structure and V.B Content; Table I; perplexity definition and explicit no-split paragraph.

title: CLoSD: Closing the Loop between Simulation and Diffusion for multi-task character control
summary: Closes a feedback loop between an autoregressive text/target-conditioned diffusion planner and an RL tracker for task sequences.
limitations: Demonstrated state-machine task sequences do not establish arbitrary task generalization or dexterous manipulation. A single lightweight tracker omits PHC’s full recovery machinery. Simulation success and selected-joint targets do not establish force-accurate human data or real-robot transfer.
method: Combines DiP, an autoregressive text/target-conditioned diffusion planner, with a universal PHC-style physics tracker. The tracker executes planned frames, then its actual simulated motion supplies the next planner prefix. Closed-loop PPO fine-tuning keeps the planner fixed and adapts the tracker across tasks. A high-level state machine switches text and target conditions when explicit task-success events occur; it is not learned open-ended task planning.
conditions: Text plus the target location of a selected body joint; actual executed motion history closes the loop. Tasks include locomotion goal reaching, striking, sitting and getting up.
data_split: DiP trains on HumanML3D and the tracker on AMASS. Text generation follows HumanML3D benchmark evaluation without a new declared proportional split. Task success uses 1,000 episodes per task with randomized placements; these are environment trials, not held-out motion-recording identities.
metrics: Task-specific success rates; FID, R-precision, MM-Dist and diversity; physical proxies measure ground penetration, floating and skating. Runtime, generation FPS and plan-length/diffusion-step ablations assess efficiency.
evaluation: Tables compare task-specific and multitask agents, open-loop execution, no fine-tuning and altered replanning lengths. Physics improves skating while feature-distribution scores can degrade relative to the unconstrained DiP planner.
evidence_locator: Sections 4.1–4.4, 5.1–5.3 and 6; Tables 1–3; task success definitions and physics metric paragraph.

title: DiffMimic: Efficient Motion Mimicking with Differentiable Physics
summary: Uses differentiable physics for efficient reference motion imitation.
limitations: Differentiable contact can produce noisy gradients and local minima, and the simulator relaxes joint limits for smoother optimization. Replaying demonstration states is a training intervention, not demonstrated autonomous recovery. Efficient reference imitation does not establish unseen motion composition, language grounding or object-interaction planning.
method: Optimizes a motion-imitation policy through differentiable Brax physics using analytical gradients propagated along simulated trajectories. The policy produces proportional-derivative joint targets from local body state and a reference phase. Demonstration replay replaces simulated states with corresponding reference states when deviation exceeds a threshold, helping avoid poor local minima and unstable long-horizon gradients. No learned world-model approximation is required.
conditions: A reference motion clip and its phase, simulated humanoid state, and known physics configuration. This is clip-conditioned control/learning, not semantic composition or text-conditioned synthesis.
data_split: Per-motion imitation setup has no dataset-level train/test recording split. Reference clips are inherited from AMP’s mixture of mocap and authored animation. Cyclic-motion policies train with four-second rollouts and are evaluated for 20-second continuation.
metrics: Average root-relative Euclidean joint pose error in meters, aligned by dynamic time warping; sample count and wall time measure training efficiency. Evaluation includes completing 20-second cyclic rollouts without falling.
evaluation: Compares DeepMimic, Spacetime Bound and AMP. Ablations compare full-horizon differentiation, short truncation, random demonstration replacement and threshold replay; per-frame errors expose behavior hidden by average imitation scores.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.4 and 5; Figures 2–4 and 6–8; Equation 4.1.

title: AMP: Adversarial Motion Priors for Stylized Physics-Based Character Control
summary: Learns motion-style rewards from unstructured clips alongside task rewards; reports emergent skill composition.
limitations: Task-specific policy/discriminator data induce dependencies that complicate transferring priors to new tasks. Discussion focuses mainly on temporal composition and identifies spatial composition as future work. Emergent behavior is simulation/task-reward evidence, not held-out free-text skill-pair generation or measured human interaction data.
method: Learns a discriminator-based motion-style reward from transitions in an unstructured reference-motion collection and combines it with a task reward in goal-conditioned reinforcement learning. Least-squares adversarial training, gradient penalty and a replay buffer stabilize imitation. Policies output joint PD targets; they need not synchronize to or select a specific reference clip. Task-directed temporal skill selection emerges from optimizing task and style together.
conditions: Character state, a task goal and an example motion dataset defining style. The high-level task reward is engineered; language is not the input condition.
data_split: Uses task-specific motion collections and per-task policy learning, not a recording-level held-out train/test composition split. Single-clip imitation compares three independent training seeds, 32 episodes per model and maximum 20-second episodes.
metrics: Normalized task returns measure task fulfillment; DTW-aligned root-relative pose error in meters measures single-clip imitation. Learning curves and sample counts evaluate efficiency/stability; qualitative sequences illustrate style and transitions.
evaluation: Demonstrates humanoid, dog and T-Rex control. Importantly, the strike prior contains walking-only and punching-only clips: the policy learns walk-then-punch without a combined demonstration. Compares tracking-based imitation and ablates discriminator gradient penalty/velocity features.
evidence_locator: Sections 5–8.5 and 9; Tables 1–3; Figure 9; Appendix task rewards.

title: InterMimicGen: Scaling Humanoid Loco-Manipulation through Self-Evolving Motion Imitation
summary: Retargets heterogeneous HOI, learns a generalist simulation tracker and iteratively retains task-preserving perturbations that execute successfully.
limitations: Validated augmentation densifies existing semantics and may favor easier objects or compound reference errors. Contact preservation treats penetration as zero distance and is not independent grasp-force certification. Real-world examples must not be described as direct transfer of one identical generalist policy across all embodiments.
method: Retargets heterogeneous human-object recordings using interaction meshes, finger-opposition constraints and contact-preserving cleanup. A generalist PPO tracker executes whole-body/object references. Self-evolution edits object placement or body posture while preserving interaction type, intended contacts, object and outcome; each round fine-tunes the tracker, executes candidates and retains successful rollouts. Accepted descendants seed further rounds rather than introducing new task semantics.
conditions: Reference body/object motion, robot morphology and explicit interaction geometry/contact intent. Outputs retargeted references and executable simulated rollouts; text-to-motion is not the learning objective.
data_split: Collection combines 9,030 InterAct and 7,029 HiPHI sequences. Tracking benchmark groups 15 objects into bimanual, sitting and grasping; evaluates trained reference execution, not a declared held-out-recording percentage. Five augmentation rounds use verified seed descendants.
metrics: Hand-contact preservation, slip, penetration, foot sliding, MPJPE, end-effector error, joint acceleration/limits; tracking success means full reference completion without failure thresholds. Reports body/object errors on successes, augmentation growth and before/after tracking success.
evaluation: Compares dexterous retargeters and per-object specialists against one generalist. Hardware paths differ: G1 uses SONIC with finger replay; Booster uses its deployment stack; Vega uses direct retargeted trajectories and slower playback.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.2–3.4 and 4.1–4.5; Tables 1–3; Appendices A, C.2, E.2–E.4, G and H.

title: Expressive Whole-Body Control for Humanoid Robots
summary: Tracks upper-body expression while lower-body velocity control enables robust locomotion, with real robot demonstrations.
limitations: Leg imitation is deliberately relaxed; root/upper-body reward scores are not full-body reconstruction accuracy. Demonstrated bottle or basketball gestures do not establish contact-rich manipulation. Hardware morphology, torque and limited environmental interaction restrict claims beyond expressive locomotion.
method: Learns expressive humanoid control by separating upper-body imitation goals from root movement commands. Human mocap is retargeted by joint-axis mapping; the lower body is free to maintain balance and locomote instead of copying incompatible leg motion. Reference-state initialization and root-command distributions sampled from real motion guide PPO exploration. Reward terms combine upper-body joint/keypoint tracking, velocity/orientation tracking and regularization.
conditions: Upper-body reference joint/keypoint trajectories, root velocity, roll/pitch/yaw and height commands, plus deployable proprioception. A text-to-motion model may supply references upstream but is separate from the motor policy.
data_split: Trains on 780 selected CMU clips totaling 13,383 seconds, filtering strong object/person/terrain interactions. Table II lists selected real-world test expressions and separate diffusion-generated examples; no random proportional or actor-disjoint split is specified.
metrics: Mean episode length (MEL), linear-velocity tracking reward (MELV), roll/pitch tracking reward (MERP), key-body tracking reward (MEK); distribution plots and real-robot demonstrations supplement these reward-based measures.
evaluation: Simulation comparison samples 10,000 trajectories across 4,096 environments. Ablations add AMP, remove reference-state initialization, sample random commands or impose full-body tracking. Unitree H1 demonstrations show expressive motion during locomotion.
evidence_locator: Sections II–IV; Tables II–IV; Figures 3–9; data curation, reward and real-world-results paragraphs.

title: Lodge: A Coarse to Fine Diffusion Network for Long Dance Generation Guided by the Characteristic Dance Primitives
summary: Global diffusion generates characteristic dance primitives; parallel local diffusion expands them into detailed long sequences, with a foot refinement component.
limitations: Kinematic FID is a statistical proxy, not physics certification. The method cannot generate detailed hand gestures or facial expressions. Long dance continuity and beat synchronization do not establish object-state dependencies, natural locomotion-to-manipulation transitions or semantic skill holdouts.
method: Uses global diffusion to generate characteristic dance primitives from long music context and local diffusion to expand them into detailed windows in parallel. Hard boundary keymotions connect adjacent windows; soft primitives are mirrored, beat-aligned and choreography-augmented to guide expressive motion. A foot-refinement block operates through forward-kinematics foot features, and a genre discriminator encourages musical-style consistency.
conditions: Music features, dance genre and generated characteristic motion primitives. Optional primitives guide local generation; this is music-conditioned choreography rather than text/object task composition.
data_split: FineDance experiments use 20 music pieces in its test set and generate 1,024-frame/34.13-second samples; reviewed text does not restate full train/validation counts. AIST++ follows Bailando’s protocol, training at 30 FPS and interpolating outputs to 60 FPS for evaluation.
metrics: Kinematic/geometric FID measure motion-feature distribution discrepancy; DIVk/DIVg measure feature variation. Beat Alignment Score measures movement/music synchronization; Foot Skating Ratio counts contact frames with excessive sliding; runtime measures generation efficiency.
evaluation: Compares FACT, MNET, Bailando and EDGE, with ablations on primitives, mirroring, beat alignment, soft cues and foot refinement. Both long FineDance and shorter AIST++ evaluations separate choreography from local motion detail.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.2–3.4, 4.1–4.4 and 5; Tables 1–5; Foot Refine Block and evaluation metric definitions.

title: A Survey on Human Interaction Motion Generation
summary: Organizes human-human, human-object and human-scene generation with datasets and evaluation; useful for backward citation chasing across interaction types.
limitations: Cross-paper numbers and taxonomies do not ensure compatible data splits, representations or evaluators. Survey capability descriptions must be checked against primary methods before asserting unseen skill composition, physical validity or deployment. No survey-wide controlled experiment establishes those claims.
method: Narrative technical survey organizes interaction motion by human-human, human-object, human-scene and mixed entities. Preliminaries compare body/object/scene representations, conditioning modalities and model families. Method discussions separate semantic coordination, spatial/physical constraints and scene context; dataset tables summarize acquisition and scope. It is a secondary taxonomy and bibliography, not a newly trained interaction generator or pooled empirical benchmark.
conditions: Not applicable as model inputs: the review catalogs text, partner motion, object/scene geometry, audio and related conditioning used by primary methods.
data_split: Not applicable: no new training/validation/test split or meta-analysis dataset is defined. A reproducible database-search query, inclusion/exclusion flow and pooled statistical protocol are not reported as a formal systematic-review methodology.
metrics: Reviews MPJPE and trajectory errors, FID/naturalness measures, diversity/multimodality, foot skating, contact/penetration, text retrieval, beat consistency and user studies. These are metrics discussed from primary papers, not newly measured survey results.
evaluation: Section 6 organizes evaluation into fidelity, diversity and condition coherence, emphasizing that interactive constraints need complementary measures. Tables compare method families and dataset properties; Section 7 discusses scaling data, richer interactions and evaluation challenges.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.4, 5, 6.1–6.4 and 7; Tables 1–9, especially Table 9 evaluation taxonomy.

title: Text-driven Motion Generation: Overview, Challenges and Directions
summary: Reviews text-to-motion through architecture and discrete/continuous representation perspectives.
limitations: The review’s broad comparative judgments do not control training data, speed hardware or evaluator differences. Its stated model limitations and dataset superlatives require primary-source verification and version context. Standard text-motion feature scores alone do not establish unseen skill-combination or interaction-state generalization.
method: Narrative overview examines text-driven human motion through two intersecting taxonomies: VAE/diffusion/hybrid architecture and discrete/continuous motion representation. It contrasts latent/token modeling, language alignment and generation/editing tradeoffs, then compares commonly used motion-language resources. The paper is a secondary conceptual review, not a new generative system or a standardized reimplementation of surveyed baselines.
conditions: Not applicable as one model condition: surveyed methods typically accept text, with optional motion context, temporal masks, style or scene cues depending on the primary work.
data_split: Not applicable: no new benchmark split is introduced and no unified train/test re-evaluation is reported. The review does not specify a reproducible search-query/inclusion-screening procedure sufficient to treat it as a formal systematic meta-analysis.
metrics: Discusses FID for generated/reference motion-feature distributions, R-precision for text retrieval, MM-Dist for paired text-motion embedding distance, diversity across outputs and multimodality for one prompt. These definitions summarize literature rather than new experimental measurements.
evaluation: Tables 1–5 compare architectural and representation advantages/limitations; Table 6 compares dataset scale, annotations and anatomical coverage. Sections 5–6 discuss scarce data, fine-grained details, ambiguous evaluation, controllability and scene-aware interaction.
